title: A mixed methods analysis of Americans' QAnon website consumption (manifest title: The Private Life of QAnon: A Mixed Methods Investigation of Americans' Exposure to QAnon Content on the Web)
screen_reason: Behavioural web-tracking study of a nationally representative US panel (N = 1,238; 21 million URL visits, Aug-Dec 2020). Reports the share of American adults who visited at least one QAnon website (3.7%) and, on the same data, the share exposed to at least one misinformation website (39.1%), plus the median share of the exposed person's news diet made up of QAnon sites. These are quantitative shares with stated denominators from behavioural data, so REACH and EXPOSURE rows qualify.

estimates.platform: Web browsing across computers, smartphones and tablets (YouGov passive URL tracking)
estimates.measure_type: % of US adults who visited at least one QAnon website during the 2020 election period
estimates.denominator: 1,238 US adults in a nationally representative YouGov web-tracking panel (weighted to national benchmarks)
estimates.definition: Participant made at least one visit to any of the 324 QAnon-related domains on the Hanley et al. (2022) list during the tracking window
estimates.misinfo_def: QAnon is described as 'an American conspiracy theory and political movement' that 'evolved to become a frequent distributor of misinformation'; misinformation itself is not separately defined by the authors
estimates.source_quote: Overall, we estimate that during the 2020 U.S. Presidential election, 3.7% (95% CI = 2.1-5.4%) of American adults were exposed to at least one QAnon website.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Database of 324 QAnon-related websites curated by Hanley et al. (2022), built by crawling all content posted on 8kun and Voat, constructing a hyperlink graph and applying automated plus manual classification; no inter-coder reliability statistic reported in this paper
estimates.moderator_quote: To identify visits to QAnon content in people's web browsing behavior, we use a database of 324 QAnon-related websites curated by Hanley et al. (2022), the largest available list of QAnon sites at the time of this writing.
estimates.notes: Headline estimate of the paper. Domain-level (not URL-level) matching; browser-only data, apps not captured (stated limitation).

estimates.platform: Web browsing across computers, smartphones and tablets (YouGov passive URL tracking)
estimates.measure_type: % of US adults who visited at least one misinformation website during the 2020 election period
estimates.denominator: 1,238 US adults in a nationally representative YouGov web-tracking panel (weighted to national benchmarks)
estimates.definition: Participant made at least one visit to a website on the misinformation-site list used by Moore et al. (2022), during the same tracking window
estimates.misinfo_def: 'a misinformation website (as defined by Moore et al., 2022)' — an untrustworthy/misinformation news domain list; the paper gives no fuller definition
estimates.source_quote: For reference, based on our data, 39.1% (95% CI = 35.0-43.1%) of American adults were exposed to a misinformation website (as defined by Moore et al., 2022) during the same time period.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: External misinformation/untrustworthy-website domain list taken from Moore et al. (2022); the list's construction is not described in this text
estimates.moderator_quote: For reference, based on our data, 39.1% (95% CI = 35.0-43.1%) of American adults were exposed to a misinformation website (as defined by Moore et al., 2022) during the same time period.
estimates.notes: This is NOT a figure cited from another paper: the authors state 'based on our data', i.e. they applied Moore et al.'s domain list to their own panel. Broader definition of the same behaviour as the QAnon row in the same country x platform cell, hence definition_variant = true.

estimates.platform: Web browsing across computers, smartphones and tablets (YouGov passive URL tracking)
estimates.measure_type: % of the median exposed person's news diet made up of QAnon websites
estimates.denominator: The news-website diet of the median QAnon-exposed panellist (the subset of the 1,238 who visited at least one QAnon site; the count of that subset is not stated)
estimates.definition: Share of that person's news-website visits that were to QAnon domains on the Hanley et al. (2022) list
estimates.misinfo_def: QAnon-related websites per the Hanley et al. (2022) taxonomy (QAnon-adjacent and QAnon-explicit domains)
estimates.n: QAnon-exposed panellists (count not stated in the text)
estimates.source_quote: For the median exposed person, only 0.16% of their news diet consisted of QAnon websites (95% quantile CI = .005, 2.8%) (Figure 1B).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Hanley et al. (2022) list of 324 QAnon domains; news-diet denominator defined by the authors' website categorisation (Dahlke et al., 2022)
estimates.moderator_quote: Panel B is the percentage of news diet that QAnon website visits made up.
estimates.notes: This is the MEDIAN of a within-person diet share among the exposed only, not a pooled share of all panellists' news diets; it therefore cannot be pooled with population-level diet-share estimates without noting the exposed-only denominator.

estimates.platform: Web browsing across computers, smartphones and tablets (YouGov passive URL tracking)
estimates.measure_type: Median number of QAnon website visits per exposed person over the ~15-week window
estimates.value_raw: the median number of QAnon website visits was 2 (95% quantile CI = 1, 117.25)
estimates.denominator: Panellists who visited at least one QAnon website (count not stated; 3.7% of 1,238)
estimates.definition: Count of visits to QAnon domains per exposed person, 24 Aug - 7 Dec 2020
estimates.misinfo_def: QAnon-related websites per Hanley et al. (2022)
estimates.n: QAnon-exposed panellists (count not stated in the text)
estimates.source_quote: Among those who did visit at least one QAnon website, the median number of QAnon website visits was 2 (95% quantile CI = 1, 117.25).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Hanley et al. (2022) list of 324 QAnon domains
estimates.moderator_quote: Among those who did visit at least one QAnon website, the median number of QAnon website visits was 2 (95% quantile CI = 1, 117.25).
estimates.notes: Intensity, not a share; median (not mean) and conditional on exposure. Highly skewed distribution (one person had 1,483 visits, next highest 125).

missed_or_uncertain: (1) '43.1% of those exposed were only exposed to one QAnon website' is a distributional statistic about the exposed subgroup, not a prevalence of misinformation in any denominator of items or people-at-risk, so no row was made. (2) Skew figures ('one person had 1,483 visits'; 'the person with the next highest number of visits had 125') are bare counts with no paired group-% and activity-% so they fail R1 and yield no CONCENTRATION row, even though the paper is clearly describing concentration of QAnon consumption in a handful of users. (3) Visit-duration statistics (45.5s for QAnon sites, 38.6s for misinformation sites, 31.0s for other sites) are not shares. (4) The extrapolated '9.5 million American adults' is a derived population count, not a share. (5) Poll figures cited from elsewhere (PRRI 30 million; YouGov 2022 41% support / 2% self-identification) are third-party and excluded by R8. (6) Subgroup/regression results (Table 1, Table 2, Figure 2, Figure 3 quantile exposure shares) are shown only as figures with no numeric values in this text, and are subgroup breakdowns of the headline rather than the headline, so no rows. (7) The manifest title ('The Private Life of QAnon...') differs from this text's title ('A mixed methods analysis of Americans' QAnon website consumption') — same study (same N = 1,238, same 21 million visits, same authors), evidently an earlier preprint title; not treated as wrong_paper.

rob.design: Passive web-tracking (all URLs visited on computers, smartphones and tablets) collected by YouGov from N = 1,238 US adults, 24 Aug - 7 Dec 2020, ~21 million URL visits; participants weighted by YouGov to be nationally representative and weights used in analysis; consented and compensated. No response rate reported. Misinformation/QAnon classification is source-level via external domain lists (324 QAnon sites from Hanley et al. 2022; misinformation sites from Moore et al. 2022) rather than in-house coding, so no inter-coder reliability statistics are reported. Qualitative component: 17 participants reviewed by researchers (3 preliminary + 14 randomly drawn from k-means clusters), no coder-agreement statistic given. Known coverage gap: browser URLs only, no in-app activity and no view of unclicked feed content.
